newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Islamic meeting urges review of Arab-Israel ties.
newsitem.headline: Islamic meeting urges review of Arab-Israel ties.

text.p: Islamic countries on Saturday urged Arab and Moslem states to reconsider relations with Israel over the building of a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem, and called on the Israelis to halt the project.
Morocco's official news agency MAP reported that the Jerusalem Committee headed by King Hassan of Morocco, which ended a meeting in Rabat on Thursday night, had said in a final statement:

"The committee exhorts Islamic states which took steps towards establishing relations with Tel Aviv in the framework of the peace process, to revise their ties with Israel including the closure of missions and offices."
The committee was set up in 1976 on the recommendation of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference to try to prevent Israel from making demographic changes to Jerusalem.

The housing project on a hill Arabs call Jabal Abu Ghneim and Israelis call Har Homa enraged Palestinians, who regard East Jerusalem, captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East War, as the future capital of an independent Palestinian state.
Palestinians and Israelis have clashed daily since building began last week.
The committee said its recommendation would stay in effect until Israel respected United Nations resolutions related to the peace process and commitments made at Oslo and Madrid.
It called on Israel "to immediately halt its settlement activities in Al-Qods (Jerusalem) city and notably in Jabal Abu Ghneim," the agency said.
The meeting asked King Hassan to send messages to Islamic heads of state asking them to make more effort to apply the terms of the final statement.

Arab and Moslem countries concerned by the committee recommendations were Mauritania, Morocco, Oman, Jordan, Qatar and Tunisia, an Arab diplomat said. He said these countries had taken steps to improve relations with Israel in recent years.
Egypt, also a member of the Islamic community, was "not concerned" because it had signed a separate accord with Israel before the 1991 Madrid Middle East peace conference, he added.

King Hassan asked the closing session to set up a fund to enable Moslems around the world to support their Palestinian brothers, the statement said. It gave no details of the fund's initial capital. A Palestinian diplomat said the fund was expected to be set up by mid-April.

It was not known why the committee delayed by 48 hours issuing its statement. But diplomats noted that the meeting coincided with talks in Morocco involving U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross, King Hassan and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
Since its creation, the committee has held 16 sessions, 15 of them in Morocco under the chairmanship of King Hassan.
Members are Bangladesh, Egypt, Guinea, Indonesia, Iran, Iraq, Jordan, Lebanon, Mauritania, Morocco, Niger, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Senegal, Syria and the Palestinian Authority.
